title: latency-trace-slice-profiling-quicknotes
body:
Purpose:
Quick working notes from a slice-based e2e trace profiling session. Goal: find predominant contributors to p95/p99 latency for short (<=128) and long (>=1024) seq-length workloads and propose low-effort mitigation experiments.

Context / why this doc exists:
- We’ve seen two recent customer tickets reporting intermittent high p95s for hosted API for text-generation.
- Standard dashboards show a bimodal sequence-length distribution; suspect interplay between batching, KV cache effectiveness, and GPU kernel selection.
- This is a lightweight, reproducible set of traces and hypotheses to drive a small experiment cycle.

Test harness / environment:
- Cluster: dedicated-gpu-pool-us-west-2 (A100-80GB), inference runtime v1.9.2-canary
- Model: open-llama-13b-quant-v2 (int8 profile), compiled with kernel-set v3.1
- Workload: two synthetic scenarios: short-chat (user tokens 8, gen 32) and doc-complete (user tokens 768, gen 512)
- Client: grpc/async, concurrency: 48, arrival pattern: Poisson (lambda tuned to ~60 RPS peak)
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry full-span capture + GPU occupancy metrics (nvidia-smi sampling) + internal KV cache hits logged per-request

Method: trace-slice workflow (what we did)
1) Capture 30m full traces during peak RPS and mark top 1% end-to-end latencies.
2) For each high-latency trace, produce a minimal slice: remove unrelated concurrent calls, keep same model/version, and replay deterministically with synthetic client that replays same tokenization and timing.
3) Run micro-profilers in isolation on slice: runtime stage timers, kernel-selection logs, queueing delays from grpc layer, GPU active/idle timestamps.
4) Aggregate stage-level percentiles and compare to representative-good traces (p50).

Representative numbers (aggregated across 120k requests):
- Overall e2e (short-chat): p50=38ms, p95=146ms, p99=370ms
- Overall e2e (doc-complete): p50=880ms, p95=2,120ms, p99=3,800ms

Per-stage median/p95/p99 breakdown (short-chat, ms):
- ingress(gRPC deserialize + auth): p50=3, p95=9, p99=28
- routing & policy (smart-routing): p50=2, p95=6, p99=18
- tokenizer + detokenize: p50=1, p95=5, p99=22
- KV prefix lookup (local cache layer): p50=0.5, p95=35, p99=210
- batching queue (time waiting to form a batch): p50=4, p95=48, p99=240
- model decode loop (kernel compute + attention): p50=24, p95=78, p99=170
- postprocess + streaming: p50=1, p95=6, p99=12
- network egress: p50=2, p95=4, p99=6

Notes on breakdown:
- Two dominant variable contributors for short-chat at p95/p99: KV prefix lookup spikes and batching queue delay.
- KV spikes correlate to cache eviction/rehash events seen on nodes with high variability in prefix lengths. Cache miss penalty measured ~180ms on average for cold prefix (includes additional model-state rehydrate steps).
- Batching queue p95/p99 driven by the batching heuristic that waits for sequence-homogeneous batches. When many long-context requests intersperse, short requests wait longer to avoid padding, causing head-of-queue delay.

Observations from trace slices (doc-complete):
- Model decode loop is dominant but not linear: p99 shows disproportionate queueing delays on GPU (queue time before kernel launch). GPU traces show short-lived preemption spikes where the CUDA stream waits ~300-900ms due to host-side kernel dispatch being blocked by a competing maintenance job (checkpoint flush) on the same node.
- Kernel selection fallback: about 7% of doc-complete traces used fallback FP32 kernels (kernel_log shows quant mismatch for some attention patterns), causing ~1.8x increase in compute time. This happens when sequence-length crosses a power-of-two boundary for a quantized-optimized kernel.

Hypotheses (ranked):
- H1: Batching heuristic is too conservative wrt seq-length variance; short requests starve when long requests are present -> increases p95 for short-chat.
- H2: KV cache eviction pattern not TTL-aware; hot prefixes evicted under memory pressure causing cold-reads at tail latencies.
- H3: Occasional host maintenance work (checkpoint uploads, cron jobs) coincides with heavy requests causing transient CUDA stream dispatch blocking.
- H4: Kernel set selection lacks a robust fallback planning leading to FP32 fallbacks on borderline shapes.

Quick experiments to run (low-effort, ordered):
- E1: Temporarily relax batching homogeneity constraint for short-chat synthetic traffic and measure p95/p99 change.
- E2: Increase KV cache size + enable LRU hysteresis on one node pool for 24h; measure cold-miss rate and tail latency.
- E3: Pin dedicated nodes for heavy doc-complete jobs (isolate maintenance cron) and compare GPU dispatch wait histograms.
- E4: Add a kernel-selection logging gate that forces quantized kernel for borderline shapes to measure perf delta (A/B test).

Data to collect / dashboards to add:
- Per-node KV cold-miss traces with request ids so we can correlate with e2e traces (add request-id to KV logs).
- Batch-formation latency histogram by seq-length bucket (0-32,33-128,129-512,513-2048).
- GPU dispatch wait histogram (ms) and correlation with system maintenance windows.
- Kernel-fallback counts per model-version and sequence-length bucket.

Immediate mitigations proposed:
- Short term: relax batching strictness for short requests in hosted API for 48 hours (E1) and monitor error rate/cost.
- Medium term: increase KV cache capacity for the busiest node pool and add LRU hysteresis (E2).
- Operational: ensure maintenance jobs are scheduled with affinity to non-serving nodes or during low-traffic windows; add preemption monitoring alert (E3).

Useful commands / snippets used in profiling (kept here for reproducibility):
- Replaying trace slice: python tools/replay_client.py --trace-id abcd1234 --concurrency 1 --preserve-timing
- Kernel log extraction: grep -E "kernel_select|fallback" /var/log/redwood/runtime/kernel.log | tail -n 200
- KV miss tracing: ./bin/kv-trace -f /var/log/redwood/kv.log --request-id abcd1234 > slice-kv.txt
- GPU dispatch histogram: python tools/gpu_dispatch_hist.py --node node-12 --since 2024-11-10T00:00:00Z

Open questions / unknowns:
- Are kernel fallback heuristics tunable at runtime without recompilation? (cc: @Marina)
- Can we identify a minimal batching tweak that preserves cost objectives but reduces short-request p99? (cc: @Jonah)
- Is there a lower-cost caching option (e.g., a small L1 cache per worker) that avoids cold rehydrates entirely for short-chats?

Action items (owners):
- Jonah: run E1 (batching relax) in canary and post results to ticket INF-876 (due 2024-11-22)
- Marina: explore kernel-selection gate and run A/B microbenchmark (due 2024-11-25)
- Evan: schedule maintenance isolation and add dispatch-wait alert to console dashboards (due 2024-11-20)
- Aisha: collect trace slices for next 3 p99 events and attach to confluence playbook (ongoing)

Appendix: short raw trace example (sanitized):
- trace-id: abcd1234
- e2e: 372ms
  - ingress: 4ms
  - batching-wait: 118ms
  - kv-cold-read: 187ms (rehydrate+state load)
  - decode: 42ms
  - post: 6ms

Bottom line:
- Headline contributors to p95/p99 are not a single stage — they are interaction effects between batching, cache behavior, and occasional host-level interference. Solve fastest wins (batching tweak + cache hysteresis) then iterate on kernel-selection and maintenance scheduling.

References / links:

Notes to self: keep these handwritten-style notes in Drive for quick iteration; move a distilled runbook to Confluence once we have stable mitigations.
